note: RUBRIC_SLIM_SPEC batch: old U4 L3, L6, L7-8 (probability, random variables; NEW Unit 2). CB probability FRQs score: the correct probability with supporting work, the interpretation as a long-run relative frequency in context, and a decision justified by the computed value — one point each. Applied with scripts/rubric-slim-apply.mjs. Revised after the Codex review: requested statistical ideas restored under the cap-5 rule; P and I made disjoint (I = neither idea / central idea wrong).

scoringGuide.E: Explains that people avoid long runs of the same outcome, while truly random sequences contain longer streaks than people expect.
scoringGuide.P: Gets one side (what humans do, or what random data does) but not the other.
scoringGuide.I: Describes random as balanced / exactly 50-50, or never mentions streaks.

scoringGuide.E: Explains that each flip is independent, so the coin is not 'due' and the next flip is still 50-50, and that the Law of Large Numbers is about the long-run proportion, not the next single flip.
scoringGuide.P: Gets independence (the next flip is still 50-50) but misstates or omits the Law of Large Numbers, or explains the long-run law without saying the next flip is still 50-50.
scoringGuide.I: Says the coin is due / things balance out in the short run, with neither idea right.

scoringGuide.E: Interprets 20% as: if many albums were randomly selected from the store's sales, about 20% would be jazz in the long run, and explains that this rate can be used for predictions beyond the 2,105 sales a raw count is tied to.
scoringGuide.P: Gives the long-run interpretation without saying why it is more useful than the count, or says why a rate generalizes without the long-run interpretation.
scoringGuide.I: Neither idea: says exactly 20% will be jazz, or never connects probability to long-run behavior.

scoringGuide.E: Sample space {red, blue, green} (or the 20 marbles); P(blue) = 5/20 = 0.25, interpreted as about 25% of many selections being blue in the long run; P(not red) = 1 - 8/20 = 0.60 using the complement; expected green = 100 x 7/20 = 35.
scoringGuide.P: Four of the five are correct; one is missing or wrong (commonly no long-run interpretation, or 35 stated as a guaranteed count).
scoringGuide.I: Two or more of the five are missing or wrong.

mistakes.Forgetting to calculate total outcomes (: Giving P(blue) without the interpretation as a long-run relative frequency

scoringGuide.E: Defines independent (one event occurring does not change the other's probability) and mutually exclusive (cannot both occur), concludes two events with positive probabilities cannot be both, and gives the reason: if they cannot happen together, one occurring makes the other impossible, which changes its probability (equivalently P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) > 0).
scoringGuide.P: Three of the four are correct; commonly the conclusion is asserted with no reason, or one definition is muddled.
scoringGuide.I: Claims positive-probability events can be both, or fewer than two of the four are correct.

scoringGuide.E: Says one check is enough because P(A|B) = P(A), P(B|A) = P(B), and P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) are equivalent conditions.
scoringGuide.P: Says one check is enough but does not name the equivalent conditions, or names the conditions without committing to whether one check suffices.
scoringGuide.I: Says every condition must be checked, or gives no reasoning about equivalence.

scoringGuide.E: Compares P(A)P(B) = 0.15 with the given P(A and B) = 0.15 and concludes independent; uses P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) = 0.65.
scoringGuide.P: Three of the four are correct; one is missing or wrong (commonly the intersection not subtracted, or the product computed but not compared).
scoringGuide.I: Two or more of the four are missing or wrong.

scoringGuide.E: Discrete = countable values with gaps; continuous = any value in an interval; gives an example of each and explains why it fits. The examples need not be original; a correct example with its reason earns the point.
scoringGuide.P: Both definitions are right but the examples are missing or unexplained, or one definition is muddled.
scoringGuide.I: Confuses the two types, or gives examples with no definitions.

mistakes.Using examples from the video instead of: Giving an example of only one type

scoringGuide.E: E(X) = (1/3)(10000) + (1/3)(1000) + (1/3)(0) = $3,666.67 with the work; interprets it as the long-run average winnings per game; recommends playing because $3,666.67 exceeds the $3,000 fee (expected profit about $667). The 1/3 probabilities are implied by the calculation.
scoringGuide.P: Two of the three are correct; one is missing (commonly a yes/no with no comparison to $3,000, or no long-run interpretation).
scoringGuide.I: Fewer than two are correct: e.g. a wrong expected value with a decision that has no reasoning.

scoringGuide.E: Net profits 8, 1, -2 with probabilities 1/6, 1/6, 4/6; E(X) = (1/6)(8) + (1/6)(1) + (4/6)(-2) = about $0.17; interprets the positive expected value as favoring the player in the long run, so the game is not fair from the carnival's side. A tidy table strengthens the answer.
scoringGuide.P: Three of the four are correct; one is missing or wrong (commonly gross winnings used instead of net, or P(other) = 1/6).
scoringGuide.I: Two or more of the four are missing or wrong.
